definition: The top layer of a layered application: the code that talks to users or other programs, such as HTTP views, command-line handlers and templates. It translates requests into calls on the layers below and formats their results.
example: A Flask view that reads JSON from a request, calls a service and returns a JSON response.

definition: The layer that coordinates one use case at a time: it loads objects, calls domain logic, saves the results, and handles transactions, permissions and side effects such as sending email. Martin Fowler calls it the service layer. It should hold orchestration, not business rules.
example: apply_discount(repo, oid, code) looks up the discount percentage, loads the order, calls order.apply_discount and saves the order.

definition: The layer holding the business rules and concepts of an application, written in the terms the business uses, with no knowledge of HTTP or storage. It is meant to be the most stable and most reusable code.
example: Order.apply_discount refusing to discount a closed order is domain-layer code.

definition: The bottom layer of a classic layered application: code that stores and retrieves data or talks to external systems, such as SQL queries, ORM mappings, files and third-party APIs.
example: SqlOrderRepository, which runs SELECT and UPDATE statements against the orders table, belongs to the data layer.

definition: A layering rule in which each layer may call only the layer directly beneath it, never skipping one. It hides each layer fully behind the next but can force pass-through code.
example: Under strict layering a view must go through the service layer even to read one row.

definition: A layering rule in which a layer may call any layer below it, skipping intermediate ones, while upward calls stay forbidden. It needs less pass-through code but lets more code depend on low layers.
example: A reporting view reading directly from the data layer, bypassing the service layer, is allowed under relaxed layering.

definition: An anti-pattern in layered systems where requests fall straight through every layer with no logic added on the way, so the layers add files and indirection without adding value. A few such paths are normal; most requests looking like this suggests relaxing or simplifying the layering.
example: get_user_view calls UserService.get_user, which only calls UserRepository.get_user.

definition: A domain model whose objects hold both data and the behaviour that enforces their rules, so callers ask an object to do something rather than changing its fields directly. It is the opposite of an anaemic domain model.
example: order.cancel() raises an error if the order has already shipped.

definition: A way of organising business logic as one procedure per request or use case, which does all the work for that action directly. Fowler describes it as a simple alternative to a domain model, suited to applications with little logic.
example: A single function that reads an order, checks the code, computes the new total and writes it back.

definition: Organising code into top-level folders by business feature (orders, users), with each feature's views, services, model and repository together inside. Most changes touch one feature through every layer, so this keeps related code side by side.
example: orders/ containing views.py, services.py, model.py and repo.py.

definition: Organising code into top-level folders by layer (views, services, repos), each holding that layer's code for every feature. A single feature change then means edits in several distant folders.
example: views/orders.py, services/orders.py and repos/orders.py all changing to add a gift message.

definition: A Python tool that checks the imports in a codebase against rules (contracts) written in a config file and fails if any import breaks them. Running it in CI turns architecture rules into a failing build.
example: A layers contract listing shop.presentation above shop.domain makes lint-imports fail if domain code imports presentation code.

definition: A rule given to Import Linter about which imports are allowed. A layers contract forbids lower layers importing higher ones; an independence contract forbids any imports, direct or indirect, between listed modules; a forbidden contract blocks imports from some modules to others.
example: A forbidden contract stopping shop.core from importing flask.

definition: In web frameworks such as Flask and Django, the function (or class) that handles requests for one URL and returns the response. In a layered design it should be a thin translator between HTTP and a use case.
example: discount_view parses the JSON body and calls services.apply_discount.

definition: A common Django style in which ORM model classes hold the business logic as methods, rather than putting it in views or separate services.
example: invoice.mark_paid() implemented as a method on the Invoice model.

definition: Django's automatically generated web interface for viewing and editing the data in your models. It is built around ORM models, so plain domain classes need mapping to use it.
example: Registering Supplier with admin.site.register gives instant create, edit and list pages.

definition: A Django helper class that builds a web form, with validation, directly from an ORM model's fields.
example: class SupplierForm(ModelForm) with Meta.model = Supplier generates fields for every Supplier column.

definition: A web framework for the Ruby language. Like Django, it uses the Active Record style, where model classes both map database rows and hold behaviour.
The seven-layer reference model for network communication (physical up to application). It is a well-known example of layered responsibilities, although real network stacks do not follow it strictly.
The four-layer model (link, internet, transport, application) on which the internet's protocols are organised. Like the OSI model, it is an example of layering in networking.

Deploying the layers of an application as separate physical tiers, such as a browser, an application server and a database server. Layers in this module are logical code structure; deploying them as separate tiers is a separate decision.
A program that runs on a schedule or on demand to process many records at once, without a user waiting, rather than handling one web request.
example: A nightly job re-pricing every abandoned basket.

definition: Checking whether an identified user is allowed to perform a particular action, such as discounting someone else's order. It is distinct from authentication, which checks who the user is.
Checking who a user is, for example by password or single sign-on. In DDD terms it is usually a generic subdomain: important, but best bought or reused rather than built.
A bug where the result depends on the timing of two concurrent operations, such as two requests that both read a value and then both write, so one change overwrites the other.
example: Two requests both read total = 100, both apply a discount and both save; one discount is lost.

definition: A Python exception raised when code reads a local variable before it has been assigned. Python decides a name is local if it is assigned anywhere in the function, even in a branch that did not run.
example: Reading new after an if-branch that assigns it was skipped raises UnboundLocalError.

definition: Code that converts objects into a format for sending or storing, such as JSON, and often back again.
example: An OrderSerializer turning an Order into {"id": 42, "total": "90.00"}.

definition: Methods that only read (get) or write (set) one field of an object. A class made mostly of them exposes every internal field and hides little.
example: get_rate(), set_rate(), get_currency(), set_currency().

definition: Coordinating a sequence of steps performed by other code, for example load, call the domain, save, then send an email. In a layered design this is the application layer's job.
In hexagonal architecture, the centre of the application: the domain model and the use cases. It imports no framework, database driver or SDK and talks to the outside only through ports it defines.
example: core/model.py and core/services.py, which import nothing from Flask or SQLAlchemy.

definition: An interface that the application core defines, in its own terms, for one purpose of talking with the outside world. Driving ports are how outside code calls the core; driven ports are what the core calls out through, implemented by adapters.
example: OrderRepository with get(oid) and add(order) is a driven port.

definition: Code outside the application core that connects a port to one specific technology, translating in both directions. Adapters depend on the core; the core never imports them.
example: SqlOrderRepository implements the OrderRepository port using SQLAlchemy.

definition: In hexagonal architecture, an adapter on the side that starts the conversation: it receives input from outside and calls into the core through a driving (primary) port.
example: A Flask view that turns an HTTP request into a call to PlaceOrder.

definition: In hexagonal architecture, an adapter that the core calls out to through a driven (secondary) port, such as a database repository, a mailer or a payment client.
example: A Postgres repository implementing OrderRepository.

definition: An architecture described by Jeffrey Palermo in 2008: the domain model at the centre, wrapped in rings of domain services and application services, with UI, infrastructure and tests in the outer ring. Dependencies point inwards.

Robert C. Martin's 2012 architecture of concentric circles: entities in the centre, then use cases, then interface adapters, then frameworks and drivers, governed by the Dependency Rule that source code dependencies point only inwards.

Clean architecture's central rule: source code dependencies can only point inwards, so nothing in an inner circle may name anything in an outer one, whether a function, class, variable or data format.
example: A use case may not import sqlalchemy or read flask.request.

definition: One thing a user or system can do with the application, such as "place an order", and the code that carries it out. In clean architecture the use-case circle holds this application-specific logic around the entities.
example: PlaceOrder loads an order, calls order.place(), saves it and notifies.

definition: The clean-architecture ring between use cases and frameworks: controllers, presenters and gateways that convert data between the form use cases want and the form external tools want.
The outermost ring of clean architecture: the web framework, database, UI and other external tools. Little code is written here beyond glue.
In clean architecture, an interface adapter that turns a use case's output into the form a particular UI needs, such as a view model or JSON.
An object that wraps access to an external resource, such as a database or another system, behind a simple interface. In clean architecture, gateways live in the interface-adapters ring.

A test double with a real but simplified working implementation, such as a repository backed by a dictionary instead of a database. Tests then check what ended up stored rather than which methods were called.
example: FakeRepo storing orders in a dict keyed by id.

definition: An ORM object that tracks the objects loaded and changed in one unit of work and writes them to the database when the transaction is committed.
example: session.commit() in SQLAlchemy flushes pending changes and commits.

definition: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, the standard internet protocol for sending email between servers.
Software that stores messages from producers until consumers process them, so the two do not have to be available at the same time. A durable queue keeps messages on disk so they survive restarts.
example: Orders publishing OrderPlaced to a queue that a Billing worker reads later.

definition: A component that delivers events or commands from the code that publishes them to the handlers subscribed to them, so publishers do not need to know who listens.

A pattern for reliably publishing events: in the same database transaction that saves the state change, also save the event to an outbox table; a separate relay process then delivers it, retrying until it succeeds. State and event can no longer get out of step.
example: Committing the placed order and an OrderPlaced outbox row together, then a relay sending it to a queue.

definition: A 2020 book by Harry Percival and Bob Gregory, free online as "Cosmic Python", that builds a Flask and SQLAlchemy app using repositories, a unit of work, a service layer and a message bus.
A Java library for writing unit tests that check architecture rules, such as which packages may depend on which.

An approach to software, set out in Eric Evans' 2003 book, that puts the main design effort into modelling a complex business domain together with the people who understand it. It has strategic parts (bounded contexts and how they relate) and tactical building blocks (entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, repositories).
A person who deeply understands the business area the software serves, such as an underwriter or a freight planner. DDD has developers model the domain in close collaboration with them.
The part of DDD about carving a large domain into bounded contexts, deciding how they relate, and choosing where to invest modelling effort.
The part of DDD that supplies building blocks for the model inside one bounded context: entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events and repositories.
In DDD, a shared vocabulary that developers and domain experts use in conversation, documents and the code itself, consistent within one bounded context.
example: If underwriters say a policy is "bound", the code says policy.bind(), not policy.set_status(3).

definition: A domain object defined by an identity that persists while its attributes change, such as a customer or a booking. Two entities with identical attributes but different ids are different things.
example: A booking that keeps reference BK-1042 while its dates and guests change.

definition: An object whose state cannot change after it is created. It can be shared freely because nothing can alter it behind your back.
example: A frozen dataclass raises FrozenInstanceError if you try to assign to one of its fields.

definition: A rule that must always hold for some data, such as "an order has at most 50 lines". In DDD, the aggregate root enforces its aggregate's invariants.

A cluster of entities and value objects treated as one unit for changes, with one aggregate root that outsiders must go through. It is the boundary for consistency and for locking: a common guideline is to change only one aggregate per transaction.
example: An Order with its OrderLines and shipping Address, where code calls order.add_line and never edits the lines list directly.

definition: The single entity in a DDD aggregate that outside code may reference and call. It enforces the invariants of the whole aggregate.
example: Order is the root of the Order aggregate; OrderLine objects are reached only through it.

definition: A record that something meaningful happened in the domain, named in the past tense, which other parts of the system can react to.
example: OrderPlaced(order_id=42), which a stock handler uses to reserve stock.

definition: A way to stop concurrent updates overwriting each other without holding locks while a user works: each row has a version number, and an update succeeds only if the version is still the one that was read. If 0 rows are updated, someone else changed it first.
example: UPDATE orders SET version = 8 WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7 updating 0 rows signals a conflict.

definition: Slowdown caused when many threads or transactions need the same lock, row or version at once and have to wait for each other (lock waits) or retry after conflicts. Heavy contention makes a program slow even when the CPU is idle.
example: Every order for a popular product locking the same stock row at peak time.

definition: A protocol for committing one transaction across several databases or services: a coordinator first asks all participants to prepare, then tells them all to commit or all to abort.

A transaction isolation level, PostgreSQL's default, where each statement sees only data committed before it began. Stronger levels such as Serializable may instead abort a conflicting transaction with a serialization error.

An error a database raises when it aborts a transaction at the Repeatable Read or Serializable isolation level because a concurrent transaction changed the same data, instead of letting the two silently overwrite each other. The application is expected to retry the whole transaction.
example: In PostgreSQL it reports 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' with SQLSTATE 40001.

definition: In DDD, a boundary within which one model and one ubiquitous language apply consistently. The same word, such as "customer", can mean different things in different contexts.
example: Sales' Customer has a lead score; Billing's Account has payment cards; both share a customer id.

definition: A DDD description of how bounded contexts relate: which is upstream (supplies a model) and which downstream (consumes it), and which relationship pattern, such as conformist or anti-corruption layer, connects them.
A context-mapping pattern where two teams share and jointly evolve a small part of their models.
A context-mapping pattern where the upstream team plans its work to serve the downstream team's needs.
A context-mapping pattern where the downstream team simply adopts the upstream model as it is, without translating it.
A translation layer at the edge of a bounded context that converts another system's model into your own, so its concepts never leak into your code.
example: LegacyCrmAdapter mapping CUST_NO and NM_FULL into your Customer(customer_id, name).

definition: A context-mapping pattern where an upstream context offers a documented public protocol or API for any downstream context to use.
A well-documented shared format, such as a public JSON schema, that contexts use to exchange information.
In DDD, one area of the overall business problem. Subdomains are classed as core, supporting or generic to decide where to spend effort.
The part of the business that makes it distinctive and gives it an edge, where DDD says to invest the best people and richest modelling.
example: Dynamic pricing for a freight company.

definition: A part of the business that is needed and specific to it, but not a differentiator, so it deserves only moderate modelling effort.
example: An internal approval workflow.

definition: A capability that does not differentiate this business and can be bought or reused rather than modelled, though it may be core to another business.
example: Login handled by an off-the-shelf identity provider.

definition: A single model of a concept, such as Customer, that every department and system must share. DDD argues it tends to satisfy none of them and prefers separate models per bounded context.
Customer relationship management: software that stores a company's customers, contacts and sales activity.
Unified Modeling Language: a standard set of diagram notations for describing software, such as class and sequence diagrams.
In Python, an object whose hash value never changes and that can be compared for equality, so it can be a dict key or set member. Mutable objects such as lists are unhashable.
Stock-keeping unit: an identifier for one specific product that a business stocks.

David Parnas's 1972 principle for dividing a program into modules: give each module one design decision that is likely to change, and hide it behind an interface so the change stays inside that module.
example: One module hides how lines are stored; if the format changes, only that module changes.

definition: Keyword in context: an index listing every keyword of each line with its surrounding words, by rotating each line. Parnas used a KWIC program as his example in the 1972 information-hiding paper.
John Ousterhout's term for a module with a small, simple interface that hides a lot of functionality. Deep modules reduce what other code must know.
example: Python's open(), one call that hides buffering, encodings and operating-system file handles.

definition: Ousterhout's term for a module whose interface is nearly as complicated as its implementation, so it hides little and adds cost.
example: A class of get_x, set_x, get_y, set_y accessors.

definition: Python's convention that a module or name starting with _ is internal and should not be used from outside its package. Python does not enforce it.
example: billing/_tax.py is internal to billing.

definition: The file that makes a folder a regular Python package and runs when the package is imported. It is often used to re-export the package's public API.
A list in a Python module naming what from module import * exports. It also documents the intended public names, but does not block explicit imports of other names.
example: __all__ = ["create_invoice", "Invoice"]

definition: Robert C. Martin's six principles for grouping classes into packages and arranging dependencies between them, including the Acyclic, Stable Dependencies and Stable Abstractions principles.
Martin's rule that the dependency graph between packages must contain no cycles. Packages in a cycle behave as one and must be changed, tested and released together.
Martin's rule that a package should be as abstract as it is stable, so that stable packages can be extended through their interfaces without being modified.
A diagram or data structure with one node per module or package and an arrow from each one to everything it imports.
A loop of dependencies, such as orders importing billing while billing imports orders. In Python it can cause ImportError at import time; even when the code runs, it ties the modules together.
example: orders → billing → customers → orders.

definition: Martin's measure of how abstract a package is: the number of abstract classes and interfaces divided by the total number of classes, from 0 to 1.
example: A package with 2 Protocols and 2 concrete classes has abstractness 0.5.

definition: In Martin's package metrics, the ideal line where abstractness plus instability equals 1. The distance from it shows how far a package strays from the Stable Abstractions Principle.

Martin's name for packages that are both stable and concrete: many things depend on them, yet they offer no abstractions to extend, so every change hurts. Rarely changing code, such as a string library, is harmless there.
Martin's name for packages that are both abstract and unstable: interfaces that nothing depends on or implements.
The Python exception raised when an import cannot be completed, for example when from orders import Order runs before Order has been defined.
A constant in Python's typing module that is False at runtime but treated as True by static type checkers, so imports placed under if TYPE_CHECKING: are seen by the checker but never executed.
A messaging style where code publishes events without knowing who receives them, and interested handlers subscribe to the event types they care about.
example: orders publishes OrderPlaced; billing subscribes, so orders never imports billing.

definition: One deployable application split into modules with enforced boundaries, each with a public API and private internals. It gives much of the code-level independence of microservices without network calls or separate deploys.
example: Shopify's core Rails app split into components checked by Packwerk.

definition: How much of a system is affected when one change or failure goes wrong. Good module boundaries keep it small.
A transaction spanning several databases or services, which must all commit or all abort. It is much harder and slower than a transaction in one database.

Shopify's open-source static analysis tool for Ruby that checks references between packages against each package's declared dependencies. Existing violations are recorded in a per-package to-do file so only new ones fail.
A recorded list of rule violations that already exist when a check is introduced. The check fails only on violations not in the list, and the team shrinks the list over time.
example: import-linter's ignore_imports or Packwerk's package_todo.yml.

definition: A package your project lists and imports itself, as opposed to the packages those packages pull in.
Fixing a dependency to one exact version, such as django==5.0.6, so every install gets the same code.
Recording a cryptographic hash for each package file in the lock file and refusing to install any file whose hash differs, so a tampered or substituted file is rejected.
A Python tool whose pip-compile command turns a list of top-level dependencies into a fully pinned requirements file, optionally with hashes.
A Python packaging and dependency manager that records exact resolved versions in poetry.lock.
A fast Python package and project manager whose uv lock command writes a lock file of exact versions.
An open-source bot that opens pull requests to keep dependencies up to date, configurable across many package managers.
When two of your dependencies need incompatible versions of the same third package, so no single version satisfies both. In Python one environment can hold only one version of each package.
example: A needs lib<2 and B needs lib>=2.

definition: Publishing a malicious package with a name close to a popular one, hoping people install it by mistyping.
example: A package called reqeusts imitating requests.

definition: The modules that ship with Python itself, such as decimal, warnings and pathlib, available without installing anything.
The Python package for Google's Protocol Buffers, a language-neutral format for serialising structured data. Like any distribution, only one version of it can be installed in one Python environment.
Copying a third-party package's source into your own project instead of installing it, sometimes renamed so it does not clash with another installed version.
A Python module written in C (or a similar language) and compiled, used for speed or to wrap a C library. It is harder to rename or vendor than pure Python.
The directory in a Python environment where installed third-party packages live, one installed version of each.
A helper process deployed alongside an application and talking to it locally, often used to isolate a component with its own dependencies.
Designing an interface so the common case needs only simple calls, while advanced options are available but stay out of the way until needed.
example: requests.get(url) for most uses; sessions, adapters and hooks when you need them.

definition: A Python parameter that cannot be passed by name. Parameters before a / in the signature are positional-only (PEP 570, Python 3.8), so their names can be changed freely.
example: def clamp(x, lo, hi, /) cannot be called as clamp(x=5, ...).

definition: An API that takes bare True or False positional arguments, so a call such as send(msg, True, False) is unreadable at the call site.
A signed digital document that proves a server's identity during a TLS (HTTPS) connection. Verifying it by default stops connections to impostor servers.
The most widely used PostgreSQL database driver for Python. Its exceptions, such as OperationalError, are specific to that driver.
A compiled programming language from Google. Its specification leaves map iteration order unspecified, and the standard runtime deliberately varies it so programs do not rely on one order.
Under Semantic Versioning, versions starting 0. are for initial development: anything may change at any time and the public API should not be considered stable.
example: A library going from 0.27.3 to 0.28.0 may remove a function.

definition: Python's rules deciding whether each warning is ignored, shown once, shown every time or turned into an error, based on its category and where it came from.
example: python -W error turns all warnings into exceptions.

definition: An empty marker file that a Python package includes (PEP 561) to tell type checkers it ships inline type hints.
A package of .pyi files that supply type hints for another package without its code.
example: types-requests provides stubs for requests.

definition: Code examining other code at runtime, such as reading a function's parameter names with inspect.signature.
Frequently asked questions: a list of common questions with answers, such as the one on the Semantic Versioning site.
In specifications such as Semantic Versioning, a capitalised MAY marks something optional and permitted, following the definitions in RFC 2119.
A library that wraps calls to a remote service so other code can use it like ordinary functions.

A short document recording one architecturally significant decision: its context, the decision and its consequences. Popularised by Michael Nygard in 2011, ADRs are usually numbered Markdown files kept in the repository.
example: docs/adr/0007-events-orders-billing.md

definition: A Markdown template for ADRs that adds a considered-options section with pros and cons for each alternative.
A design decision that is costly to reverse, affects the system's structure or important qualities, or is likely to be questioned later.
example: Choosing the primary database; not naming a variable.

definition: The status of an ADR whose decision has been replaced by a later ADR. The old record is kept as history, pointing to its replacement.
example: ADR 0004 marked "Superseded by 0019".

definition: A regular publication by the consultancy Thoughtworks rating tools and techniques in rings from Adopt to Hold.
A lightweight plain-text formatting syntax, using marks like # for headings and * for emphasis, widely used for documentation in repositories.
Jeff Bezos's term for a consequential decision that is very hard to reverse, which deserves slow, careful thought.
example: Choosing the primary database for ten years of data.

definition: Jeff Bezos's term for a decision that is easy to reverse, so it should be made quickly.
example: Picking a logging library that is already wrapped behind an adapter.

definition: The idea of delaying an irreversible decision until the point where not deciding would start to cost more, so it is made with the most information available.

An architecture that supports guided, incremental change across several dimensions, as defined in Ford, Parsons and Kua's Building Evolutionary Architectures. Fitness functions guard the properties that must survive the changes.
An objective, preferably automated, check that an architectural characteristic still holds, run like a test so it fails the build when the architecture drifts.
example: An import-linter contract in CI that fails if shop.domain imports flask.

definition: A quality a system must have beyond its features, such as performance, layering, security or deployability.
A test that sends a realistic or heavy volume of traffic to a system to measure response times and find where it slows down. The tool that sends the traffic is a load generator.
A unit of data size, 1000 bytes (or 1024 bytes in older usage), written KB or kB.
example: 250 KB is about a quarter of a megabyte.

definition: The total size of the JavaScript and other files a web page must download, which affects how quickly it loads.

Making a large change all at once rather than gradually; for a rewrite, replacing a whole system with a new one built separately and switched over in one go. It delays feedback and value until the end and risks losing undocumented behaviour.
An object or layer that offers one simple interface in front of a more complex system. In a strangler fig migration it decides whether each request goes to the old or the new code.
Running an old and a new implementation side by side on the same inputs, serving the old result and logging differences, until the new one is trusted.
example: Pricing every quote with both engines and investigating each mismatch.

definition: GitHub's open-source Ruby library for parallel runs: it runs a control and a candidate implementation, returns the control's result and records differences. Ports exist for other languages.
Martin Fowler's 2015 advice to start a new system as a well-structured monolith and extract services later, once the right boundaries are understood.
Deliberately building a design you expect to throw away when the system outgrows it, investing accordingly.
example: eBay moving from Perl to C++ to Java as it grew.

definition: Melvin Conway's 1968 observation that organisations which design systems tend to produce designs that copy their own communication structures.
example: Separate frontend, backend and database teams producing a system split into those three layers.

definition: Deliberately organising teams to match the architecture you want, so Conway's law works in your favour.
example: Forming one cross-functional team each for search, checkout and accounts.

definition: A team that has all the skills needed to deliver a feature end to end, such as frontend, backend and data.
Running several versions of a service's API at once so clients can migrate gradually when it changes incompatibly.
A Python import written relative to the current package, such as from ._tax import rate. A dynamic import is one chosen at runtime, for example with importlib.import_module.

In any layered design, higher layers build on the services of lower ones and sit nearer the user. In a layered application, presentation is at the top and data at the bottom; in a network stack, the application layer sits above transport, IP and the link. In application code, a higher layer may import a lower one; a lower layer must never import a higher one.
example: presentation importing application is allowed; data importing presentation breaks the rule.

definition: Software structured as layered architecture: code split into layers by kind of concern, with dependencies allowed only from higher layers to lower ones.
example: A shop app whose views call services, which call domain classes, which are saved by repositories.

definition: A name in a module or package that other code is meant to use, as opposed to an internal one. In Python, public names have no leading underscore and are often listed in __all__ or re-exported from __init__.py.
example: create_invoice is a public name of billing; _tax.vat_rate is not.
